objective: Make tag-two better at achieving its purpose.
summary: The repository describes tag-two as a tiny experiment in persistent, agent-assisted problem solving. The current implementation allows an agent to investigate a repository and propose a task graph, but the initial dogfood runs revealed gaps in research depth and decomposition quality. The agent often mirrors the most salient text in its context rather than producing a useful decomposition. The system lacks mechanisms to ensure complete research or improve task relevance. The README outlines lessons from prior attempts and identifies remaining uncertainties, such as whether complete research improves decomposition or merely changes which text gets mirrored.

nodes.title: Ensure complete research before decomposition
nodes.reason: The agent often stops reading files prematurely, leading to incomplete research and poor task proposals. Ensuring complete research is foundational to improving decomposition quality.
evidence: README.md:91-97 — Assessment of the first dogfood run highlights incomplete research as a key issue.
README.md:132-136 — The agent ignored explicit instructions to paginate files, demonstrating the need for a systemic solution.

nodes.title: Improve evidence citations in task proposals
nodes.reason: Broad file citations (e.g., entire files) lack specificity and do not justify tasks. Narrow, line-specific citations would make task proposals more actionable and credible.
evidence: README.md:88-89 — The summary notes that evidence citations are broad file ranges rather than specific observations.
src/graph.js:12-13 — Validation enforces evidence citations but does not ensure their specificity.

nodes.title: Clarify the research summary in the graph
nodes.reason: The research summary should clearly distinguish inspected tests from verified runtime behavior and identify remaining uncertainties. This would help humans evaluate the graph's usefulness.
evidence: README.md:87-88 — The summary does not clearly distinguish inspected tests from verified runtime behavior.
src/graph.js:55-56 — The HTML rendering includes the research summary but does not enforce clarity.

nodes.title: Expand test coverage for runtime behavior
nodes.reason: The current tests focus on file handling and validation but do not verify runtime behavior (e.g., whether the agent completes research). Expanding coverage would help identify and address gaps.
evidence: README.md:85-86 — The summary notes that runtime behavior remains unverified.
test/tag.test.js:1-301 — Existing tests cover file handling and validation but not runtime behavior.

nodes.title: Document lessons from the first dogfood run
nodes.reason: The README includes a detailed assessment of the first dogfood run, but these lessons should be formalized in the codebase to guide future improvements.
evidence: README.md:83-97 — Detailed assessment of the first dogfood run.
src/plan.js:1-153 — The planner could incorporate lessons to improve research and decomposition.

investigation.result:
1: tag-two
2: 
3: «A tiny experiment in persistent, agent-assisted problem solving.»
4: 
5: ## Run the seed
6: 
7: Requires Node.js 22+ and Git. There are no package dependencies or build step.
8: From a Git repository's root, set `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` in your environment (never
9: in a tracked file), then run:
10: 
11: ```sh
12: node /absolute/path/to/tag-two/bin/tag.js plan "Make tag-two better at achieving its purpose."
13: ```
14: 
15: An optional final argument selects another repository root. To use the shorter
16: `tag plan "objective"` command, run `npm link` in the tag-two checkout first.
17: Run the offline tests with `npm test` in that checkout.
18: 
19: The planner uses one OpenRouter model, `deepseek/deepseek-chat-v3-0324`, with
20: read-only tools to list/read/search tracked text files and inspect recent commit
21: subjects. The model chooses what to investigate; no source excerpts are selected
22: in advance. Add new source files to Git before planning. It cannot execute shell
23: commands, run tests, modify source, or work on the proposed tasks. Its claims about
24: what works are therefore explicitly unverified unless repository evidence supports them.
25: 
26: **Data boundary:** the objective and model-requested repository content are sent to
27: OpenRouter and its model provider. Use only repositories you are authorized to
28: share. Untracked files, common credential paths, symlinks, binary files and files
29: larger than 256 KiB are excluded; these filters are not a secret detector. Review
30: tracked content for embedded secrets before using the planner.
31: 
32: After investigation, open `.tag/graph.html` directly in a browser. It shows the
33: objective, research summary, task reasons and evidence, linked dependencies,
34: ready/blocked tasks, and the tool results behind the plan. `.tag/graph.json` is the
35: durable, provider-independent graph; its `run` field records model provenance,
36: reported cost (or null when unavailable), and investigation history.
37: 
38: The graph is a proposal, not an execution queue: “ready” means no graph dependencies,
39: and a human decides what happens next. Nothing runs automatically afterward.
40: Both outputs stay local and are Git-ignored via a generated `.tag/.gitignore`,
41: including when planning in another repository, because they may include repository
42: content. Existing `.tag` directories are never overwritten: preserve or move a
43: previous experiment explicitly before starting another.
44: 
45: The seed allows at most ten model requests, 4,096 output tokens per request and
46: 80,000 serialized request bytes. It checks model pricing and caps provider prices
47: at $0.50/million input tokens and $1.50/million output tokens, with no per-request
48: fee. At these limits, even conservatively counting each request byte as an input
49: token leaves the run below $1 (roughly $0.47 before small protocol overhead).
50: Unavailable models, higher prices, network errors, exhausted limits or invalid
51: graphs stop the run without automatic retries, JSON repair or fabricated tasks.
52: An output write failure can leave a partial `.tag` directory; inspect it before
53: moving it aside.
54: 
55: The first dogfood run should use the objective above exactly once. Inspect its
56: unedited graph for usefulness rather than rerunning until the answer looks good.
57: 
58: **First attempt (2026-09-15):** the command above stopped at the model-catalog
59: request because `openrouter.ai` could not be resolved (`ENOTFOUND`) in the build
60: environment. No model inference request was made and no graph was generated.
61: 
62: **First completed dogfood run (2026-09-15):** after the domain allowlist was
63: updated, one run of the unchanged planner succeeded. DeepSeek V3 0324 made three
64: model requests at a reported total cost of **$0.00399975**. It listed files and
65: read the first 200 lines of the README, all three implementation modules, and
66: the test file. It did not paginate the README, inspect history, or run tests.
67: 
68: The unedited outputs are preserved in
69: [`examples/first-dogfood/graph.json`](examples/first-dogfood/graph.json) and
70: [`examples/first-dogfood/graph.html`](examples/first-dogfood/graph.html).
71: Download/open the HTML locally to inspect it. These are explicitly archived
72: experiment artifacts, including the original repository investigation transcript;
73: normal `.tag` output remains ignored.
74: 
75: The graph proposed five tasks:
76: 
77: 1. Investigate README.md for project purpose and principles.
78: 2. Review graph validation and rendering logic (depends on 1).
79: 3. Examine the planning module for constraints and behavior (depends on 1).
80: 4. Test repository tools for file handling and security (depends on 1).
81: 5. Analyze the test suite for coverage and gaps (depends on 2, 3, and 4).
82: 
83: **Assessment: the mechanics work, but this is not yet a useful decomposition.**
84: Most tasks repeat inspection the planner already performed, without identifying
85: a demonstrated weakness or a concrete improvement to the central experiment.
86: The dependencies mostly express review order rather than necessary task results.
87: The summary does not clearly distinguish inspected tests from verified runtime
88: behaviour, or identify the remaining uncertainties. Its evidence citations are
89: broad file ranges rather than observations that justify specific work.
90: 
91: This run exposes a research-quality problem, not a need for more orchestration:
92: the agent stopped reading the README before reaching the lessons, scope limits
93: and first-success criteria, despite having requests left. It then largely
94: mirrored the files it inspected. The next experiment should address that observed
95: gap in research and decomposition, not automatically execute this graph or add
96: scheduling machinery. No tasks were executed and no extra run was made to obtain
97: a more appealing answer.
98: 
99: **Second dogfood attempt (2026-09-15, no graph):** after `read_file` was changed
100: to report partial reads, one run of the planner reached the model, investigated the
101: repository, and returned an answer that failed graph validation. The planner then
102: deleted `.tag`, so the only surviving information was the error string
103: (`Expected the original objective, a research summary, and 1–8 nodes.`). The
104: transcript and the rejected answer were gone, and a real paid run taught us nothing
105: about why it failed.
106: 
107: That is the observed need behind the next change: a failed run now writes
108: `.tag/failed-run.json` with the objective, failure message, request count, reported
109: cost, full investigation transcript and raw model answer, and keeps the directory.
110: No repair, retry or fallback was added — only the ability to see what happened.
111: 
112: **Second completed dogfood run (2026-09-15):** the same objective was run once more,
113: because the previous attempt produced no graph to assess. DeepSeek V3 0324 made three
114: requests at a reported total cost of **$0.004499**, reading `package.json` and all
115: four implementation and test files, plus the first 200 lines of the README. The
116: unedited outputs are preserved in
117: [`examples/second-dogfood/graph.json`](examples/second-dogfood/graph.json) and
118: [`examples/second-dogfood/graph.html`](examples/second-dogfood/graph.html).
119: 
120: The graph proposed five tasks:
121: 
122: 1. Improve research depth and completeness.
123: 2. Enforce stricter validation of evidence citations (depends on 1).
124: 3. Clarify the research summary (depends on 1).
125: 4. Expand test coverage for runtime behaviour (depends on 2).
126: 5. Document lessons from the first dogfood run (depends on 1).
127: 
128: **Assessment: the change failed its purpose, and the better-looking graph is
129: misleading.** The tool change worked exactly as designed — the model was told
130: `PARTIAL READ: lines 1-200 of 739. The remaining 539 lines of README.md have NOT
131: been shown. Call read_file with path "README.md" and startLine 201 to read them.`
132: and an equivalent notice for `test/tag.test.js`. It paginated neither, with seven
133: of ten requests unused. **Telling the model its view is incomplete, in explicit
134: terms that name the exact next call, did not make it finish reading.** The
135: research gap identified after the first run is therefore still open, and the
136: obvious cheap fix for it is now ruled out by evidence rather than by opinion.
137: 
138: The proposed tasks read as improvements rather than as one review task per source
139: file, and two of them cite specific line ranges instead of whole files. But this is
140: not better research. The five tasks correspond almost one-to-one to sentences in the
141: human assessment of the first run written at `README.md:83-97`, which had moved into
142: the first 200 lines the agent did read: premature reading, broad evidence citations,
143: an unclear summary, unverified runtime behaviour, undocumented lessons. The agent is
144: still mirroring the most salient text in its context. In the first run that text was
145: a file listing; in the second it was a human's critique. The apparent improvement
146: came from a human writing the analysis into the input, not from the agent producing
147: it.
148: 
149: The sharpest single observation: the agent proposed *"Improve research depth and
150: completeness — ensures the agent reads the entire README and other key files"* in the
151: same request in which it declined to read the rest of the README. It can name the
152: weakness it is exhibiting without that changing its behaviour.
153: 
154: What this rules out, and what remains open:
155: 
156: - Ruled out: passive truncation notes, and explicit directive ones, as a way to get
157:   complete research. Both were tried against a real run and both failed.
158: - Still open: whether the system should guarantee complete reading itself rather than
159:   asking the model to, and whether complete research actually improves decomposition
160:   or merely changes which text gets mirrored. These are separate questions and the
161:   second cannot be answered until the first is.
162: - Not evidenced: any need for scheduling, execution, retries, model routing or
163:   multi-generation machinery. Nothing in either run pointed at those.
164: 
165: Both runs used the objective exactly once each. No run was repeated to obtain a more
166: appealing graph, no proposed task was executed, and the archived artifacts are
167: unedited.
168: 
169: ---
170: 
171: Why this exists
172: 
173: Modern coding agents are remarkably capable when given a well-defined task.
174: 
175: The harder problem is deciding what should be done next.
176: 
177: Real projects are rarely a queue of perfectly specified independent tickets. An objective may require research before implementation. Research may reveal new work. Tasks may depend on other tasks. Some questions require humans. Some approaches fail. Priorities change as evidence accumulates.
178: 
179: "tag-two" explores a simple idea:
180: 
181: Represent that evolving understanding as a persistent graph, and let agents help investigate and evolve it.
182: 
183: The graph is not primarily a backlog.
184: 
185: It is the system's current model of the problem.
186: 
187: ---
188: 
189: The core idea
190: 
191: Start with an objective:
192: 
193: «Improve tag-two.»
194: 
195: An agent investigates the relevant repository and problem using its normal tools.
196: 
197: It then constructs a small graph representing useful next work:
198: 
199: Improve tag-two
200: │
201: ├── Understand current behaviour
202: │
203: ├── Investigate an important uncertainty
204: │
205: ├── Improve a demonstrated weakness
206: │   └── depends on investigation
207: │
208: └── Demonstrate the improvement
209: 
210: The graph persists independently of any model conversation.
211: 
212: Later, a node can be investigated or worked on by another agent. Its result changes the graph.
213: 
214: Over time:
215: 
216: objective
217:     ↓
218: investigate
219:     ↓
220: graph
221:     ↓
222: choose useful work
223:     ↓
224: agent works
225:     ↓
226: observe result
227:     ↓
228: update graph
229:     ↓
230: repeat
231: 
232: Initially, humans may perform some of those transitions manually.
233: 
234: That is intentional.
235: 
236: The experiment is to gradually discover which parts are useful to automate rather than designing the complete autonomous system in advance.
237: 
238: ---
239: 
240: The hypothesis
241: 
242: A useful agent system does not necessarily need one enormous autonomous context.
243: 
244: Instead, it can maintain durable external state describing:
245: 
246: - what we are trying to achieve;
247: - what we currently believe;
248: - what has been discovered;
249: - what remains uncertain;
250: - what work is available;
251: - what depends on what;
252: - what has already happened;
253: - where a human is required.
254: 
255: Agents can then operate on bounded pieces of that state.
256: 
257: This potentially allows different agents, models, tools and humans to collaborate without requiring a single continuous conversation.
258: 
259: The persistent graph is the continuity.
260: 
261: ---
262: 
263: The most important principle
264: 
265: The graph is the product.
266: 
267: Internal state is only useful if a human can understand it.
268: 
269: At every meaningful stage we should be able to inspect the graph and answer:
270: 
271: - What is the objective?
272: - What does the system currently think needs doing?
273: - Why?
274: - What has it learned?
275: - What is runnable now?
276: - What is blocked?
277: - What depends on something else?
278: - Where is human input required?
279: - What changed recently?
280: 
281: A JSON representation may be the durable format.
282: 
283: It must not be the primary human interface.
284: 
285: Even a crude HTML representation is preferable if it makes the system understandable at a glance.
286: 
287: ---
288: 
289: What a node represents
290: 
291: A node represents a meaningful part of the system's understanding of the problem.
292: 
293: A node may eventually represent things such as:
294: 
295: - work;
296: - investigation;
297: - a question;
298: - evidence;
299: - a decision;
300: - an outcome.
301: 
302: Do not build an elaborate type system until the implementation needs one.
303: 
304: For the first version, a node can be extremely small.
305: 
306: For example:
307: 
308: {
309:   "id": "research-current-behaviour",
310:   "title": "Understand current planning behaviour",
311:   "reason": "We need evidence about the current behaviour before changing it.",
312:   "dependsOn": []
313: }
314: 
315: Add fields only when a demonstrated use case requires them.
316: 
317: ---
318: 
319: Research before decomposition
320: 
321: One of the strongest lessons from the original TAG experiment is that decomposition quality depends on research quality.
322: 
323: A model shown a handful of arbitrary source excerpts will tend to generate work related to those excerpts.
324: 
325: That is not necessarily the same as work important to the objective.
326: 
327: For example, an objective such as:
328: 
329: «Improve TAG»
330: 
331: previously produced locally plausible tasks involving protocol fields, validation edge cases and CLI parsing.
332: 
333: Those tasks were not necessarily wrong.
334: 
335: The problem was that the system had insufficient understanding to know whether they mattered.
336: 
337: Therefore:
338: 
339: Do not confuse code inspection with understanding the objective.
340: 
341: Before decomposing a broad objective, an agent should be able to investigate enough context to understand:
342: 
343: 1. what the project is trying to achieve;
344: 2. what currently exists;
345: 3. what currently works;
346: 4. what has already been attempted;
347: 5. what important uncertainties remain;
348: 6. what would constitute meaningful progress.
349: 
350: The agent should use normal repository tools where possible:
351: 
352: - read files;
353: - search;
354: - inspect documentation;
355: - inspect tests;
356: - inspect relevant history;
357: - run safe/read-only commands where appropriate.
358: 
359: Do not recreate a coding agent's repository exploration abilities by manually assembling arbitrary source excerpts unless there is a demonstrated reason to do so.
360: 
361: ---
362: 
363: Agents are capabilities, not the state
364: 
365: An agent may be:
366: 
367: - a hosted coding agent;
368: - a model accessed through an API;
369: - a local model;
370: - a human;
371: - another orchestration system.
372: 
373: The graph should not depend on the conversational memory of any particular agent.
374: 
375: A fresh agent should be able to understand the relevant work from durable project state plus whatever repository/environment access it is given.
376: 
377: This means:
378: 
379: «Worker handoffs may be stateless. Durable project understanding cannot be.»
380: 
381: The graph owns continuity.
382: 
383: Agents temporarily contribute reasoning or work.
384: 
385: ---
386: 
387: Human involvement is normal
388: 
389: Human intervention is not a failure mode.
390: 
391: Especially during bootstrap, a human may:
392: 
393: - choose which node to work next;
394: - reject a poor decomposition;
395: - answer a question;
396: - approve a risky action;
397: - select an agent or model;
398: - inspect an outcome;
399: - decide whether evidence is sufficient.
400: 
401: If an agent lacks a permission or capability, surface that boundary.
402: 
403: Do not silently invent workarounds merely to preserve the appearance of autonomy.
404: 
405: The goal is useful orchestration, not maximum autonomy.
406: 
407: ---
408: 
409: Bounded agent work
410: 
411: Agents should usually receive bounded work.
412: 
413: A useful pattern is:
414: 
415: inspect
416: → perform one meaningful action
417: → report what happened
418: → update durable state
419: → stop
420: 
421: Avoid agents implicitly continuing through an unlimited chain of work merely because more work is available.
422: 
423: This makes behaviour easier to understand, review and recover.
424: 
425: The appropriate boundaries should emerge through experimentation rather than being specified completely now.
426: 
427: ---
428: 
429: Model choice
430: 
431: Different graph nodes may eventually benefit from different models.
432: 
433: For example:
434: 
435: - decomposition may favour concise instruction-following;
436: - difficult implementation may favour a strong coding model;
437: - summarisation may use a cheap model;
438: - research may require stronger reasoning or larger context.
439: 
440: Do not build model routing yet.
441: 
442: Start with one model/agent that works.
443: 
444: Model selection becomes part of the system only when there is evidence that it provides meaningful value.
445: 
446: One lesson from the original TAG experiment was that stronger reasoning is not automatically better for every operation.
447: 
448: A reasoning-heavy model repeatedly exhausted a structured planning output budget before producing valid JSON. Disabling reasoning for that bounded structured-planning call produced a valid graph using substantially fewer output tokens.
449: 
450: The broader lesson is:
451: 
452: Use model capability appropriate to the operation rather than simply maximising reasoning effort.
453: 
454: ---
455: 
456: Cost
457: 
458: Cost matters, particularly if graphs eventually create many agent calls.
459: 
460: But cost optimisation is not the first experiment.
461: 
462: First establish that the system produces useful work.
463: 
464: Then measure.
465: 
466: Then optimise.
467: 
468: Cheap and free models are interesting because sufficiently bounded graph nodes may allow smaller models to perform useful work.
469: 
470: That is a hypothesis worth testing later.
471: 
472: Do not compromise the initial demonstration merely to make it free.
473: 
474: ---
475: 
476: What we learned from the original TAG
477: 
478: An earlier implementation explored many of these ideas.
479: 
480: It included concepts such as:
481: 
482: - persistent graph state;
483: - graph revisions;
484: - generations;
485: - structured graph mutations;
486: - strict proposal validation;
487: - controller/worker separation;
488: - execution limits;
489: - token and cost accounting;
490: - model allowlists;
491: - provider routing;
492: - research-context construction;
493: - worker packages;
494: - acceptance gates;
495: - persistent history;
496: - HTML graph rendering.
497: 
498: Many of those ideas may eventually be useful.
499: 
500: They are not requirements for tag-two.
501: 
502: The original experiment taught us that it is easy to build sophisticated orchestration machinery before proving that the central loop is useful.
503: 
504: Several experiments became dominated by debugging the orchestration infrastructure itself:
505: 
506: - model availability;
507: - provider routing;
508: - reasoning-token behaviour;
509: - output-token ceilings;
510: - strict JSON proposal validation;
511: - research-context selection;
512: - controller-state transport;
513: - protocol/status compatibility.
514: 
515: Meanwhile the question we actually cared about was much simpler:
516: 
517: «Can the system investigate an objective and produce a useful graph that we can see?»
518: 
519: "tag-two" starts again from that question.
520: 
521: ---
522: 
523: Things we deliberately do not know yet
524: 
525: We do not yet know the correct:
526: 
527: - graph schema;
528: - node taxonomy;
529: - scheduling algorithm;
530: - mutation protocol;
531: - execution protocol;
532: - generation semantics;
533: - agent transport;
534: - model-routing policy;
535: - retry policy;
536: - prioritisation algorithm;
537: - context-building strategy;
538: - concurrency model;
539: - cost-control system;
540: - controller architecture;
541: - long-term storage architecture.
542: 
543: These are research questions.
544: 
545: Do not turn them into architecture until actual usage provides evidence.
546: 
547: ---
548: 
549: What not to build yet
550: 
551: Unless required to make the current demonstration work, do not add:
552: 
553: - autonomous multi-generation execution;
554: - controller/worker protocols;
555: - generic mutation languages;
556: - complex lifecycle state machines;
557: - provider abstraction layers;
558: - model allowlists;
559: - model routing;
560: - retries;
561: - JSON repair;
562: - elaborate cost reservation;
563: - concurrency;
564: - scheduling;
565: - prioritisation engines;
566: - background workers;
567: - remote services;
568: - authentication;
569: - web applications;
570: - plugin systems;
571: - speculative extensibility.
572: 
573: A small amount of ugly glue is acceptable.
574: 
575: Premature infrastructure is not.
576: 
577: ---
578: 
579: Bootstrap rule
580: 
581: Every iteration should make the next useful iteration less manual.
582: 
583: That is the path toward self-hosting.
584: 
585: For example:
586: 
587: Iteration 0
588: human → objective → agent → graph → human
589: 
590: Iteration 1
591: human → graph node → agent → result → human updates graph
592: 
593: Iteration 2
594: human → graph node → agent → result → system updates graph
595: 
596: Iteration 3
597: system suggests next node → human approves → agent works
598: 
599: Iteration 4
600: system handles bounded low-risk work itself
601: 
602: This sequence is illustrative, not a roadmap.
603: 
604: Do not implement later iterations until the previous behaviour exists and teaches us something.
605: 
606: ---
607: 
608: Self-hosting
609: 
610: "tag-two" should eventually help improve "tag-two".
611: 
612: This is not merely a novelty.
613: 
614: Self-hosting provides a useful feedback loop because weaknesses in the orchestration system become real problems represented inside the system itself.
615: 
616: The desired pattern is:
617: 
618: tag-two identifies useful work
619:         ↓
620: one of those tasks improves tag-two
621:         ↓
622: the improved tag-two handles the next iteration
623: 
624: A useful guiding phrase is:
625: 
626: «The graph should eventually contain the work required to remove humans from the parts of the graph where they add no value.»
627: 
628: Humans should remain where judgement, preference, authority or approval genuinely matters.
629: 
630: ---
631: 
632: Relationship to larger systems
633: 
634: This experiment is deliberately tiny.
635: 
636: A larger orchestration system such as Harbour may eventually provide interfaces, task-provider integration, richer agent dispatch, chat interaction, prioritisation and operational views around concepts like these.
637: 
638: Do not design tag-two around Harbour.
639: 
640: If the primitive is genuinely useful, integration opportunities will become obvious later.
641: 
642: tag-two should remain understandable and runnable independently.
643: 
644: ---
645: 
646: Portability
647: 
648: The underlying idea should not depend on a particular coding-agent vendor.
649: 
650: A future graph node might be worked by:
651: 
652: - Claude Code;
653: - Codex;
654: - Copilot;
655: - an OpenRouter model;
656: - a local model;
657: - Harbour;
658: - a human.
659: 
660: Do not implement all of these.
661: 
662: But avoid making the graph itself synonymous with one provider's conversation format.
663: 
664: ---
665: 
666: The first implementation
667: 
668: The first version has one job:
669: 
670: objective + repository
671:         ↓
672: agent investigates repository
673:         ↓
674: small task graph
675:         ↓
676: graph.json
677:         ↓
678: graph.html
679: 
680: Then stop.
681: 
682: No graph tasks are executed.
683: 
684: The planner should produce a small graph — roughly a handful of nodes, not an exhaustive backlog.
685: 
686: Each proposed task should answer:
687: 
688: Why is this useful for the objective?
689: 
690: Dependencies should exist only when they carry real meaning.
691: 
692: The agent should investigate the repository itself rather than receiving a manually curated approximation of it.
693: 
694: ---
695: 
696: First dogfood objective
697: 
698: Once the minimum implementation exists, run it against its own repository with:
699: 
700: «Make tag-two better at achieving its purpose.»
701: 
702: This is the first meaningful experiment.
703: 
704: Do not manually design the answer.
705: 
706: Do not repeatedly rerun the planner until it produces something we like.
707: 
708: Generate a real graph and inspect what it actually thought.
709: 
710: The important question is:

720: First success criterion
721: 
722: We should be able to run something conceptually similar to:
723: 
724: tag plan "Make tag-two better at achieving its purpose."
725: 
726: and receive:
727: 
728: .tag/
729:   graph.json

735:

737: - the proposed tasks;
738: - why they matter;
739: - dependencies;

747: 
748: What happens after that
749: 
750: Nothing automatically.
751: 
752: We inspect the graph.
753: 
754: If it is poor, that is evidence.
755: 
756: We improve the part of tag-two responsible for the weakness.
757: 
758: If it is useful, we choose one node from the graph tag-two itself produced.
759: 
760: An agent works that node.
761: 
762: Then we determine the smallest mechanism necessary to feed the result back into the graph.
763: 
764: That becomes the next implementation step.
765: 
766: Not before.

770: Development philosophy
771: 
772: Prefer:
773: 
774: - vanilla JavaScript;
775: - small modules;
776: - few dependencies;
777: - files over services where practical;
778: - explicit behaviour;
779: - inspectable state;
780: - simple commands;
781: - boring data structures;
782: - changes justified by observed needs.
783: 
784: Avoid cleverness whose value has not yet been demonstrated.
785: 
786: The project should remain small enough that one developer can understand the complete system.

789: 
790: A test for every proposed feature
791: 
792: Before adding infrastructure, ask:
793: 
794: «What happened in a real tag-two run that makes us need this?»
795: 
796: If there is no concrete answer, don't build it yet.
